newsitem.title: GERMANY: Compromise elusive for Bonn's 1997 tax bill.
newsitem.headline: Compromise elusive for Bonn's 1997 tax bill.

text.p: German government and opposition parties appear as far apart as ever on the 1997 tax bill, making it unlikely key corporate tax cuts will pass before year-end, officials said on Friday.

Failure to pass the complete package could force federal and state governments to find up to 10 billion marks ($6.54 billion) in additional spending cuts if Germany is to cut its public deficit enough to qualify for the single European currency.
"Both sides must bring something new to the table," when negotiations are reopened on Monday, a coalition source said.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and their Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners are still wooing the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), whose cooperation is crucial to the bill's passage.

But due to legal technicalities, inaction would allow both sides to achieve big political, if not financial goals: for the coalition the elimination of a wealth tax, and for the SPD the increase in aid to families with children.

The SPD is resisting government overtures because it says the bill will hurt ordinary taxpayers and families. Perhaps more importantly, it will hurt the finances of state governments, most of which are controlled by the SPD.
The SPD's leadership in the states gives it a majority in the upper house of parliament and an effective veto over the tax bill.
Talks held earlier this week ended with no sign of compromise, and government sources say Finance Minister Theo Waigel is only willing to give the negotiations one more try.
"We won't play along for weeks in this little drama," said one coalition source.

Failure to pass the bill would, however, mean another delay in Germany's plan to eliminate the corporate assets tax, which the government says is necessary to keep the country attractive for capital investment. The states are opposed because the revenues flow mainly to them.
"There is no chance of an agreement," on the corporate assets tax, said SPD parliamentarian Joachim Poss.
The government has proposed raising the states' share of value-added tax as a compensation, but the states are not satisfied with the offer.

Joachim Horster, a coalition parliamentary leader, accused the SPD of "blockade politics" that would unnecessarily burden corporations in western Germany and add new taxes in the east, where the EU has ruled the corporate assets tax will have to be introduced if it is not eliminated nationally.
The issue was postponed once before, last year, and corporations will likely have to keep waiting for relief.

In the absence of legislative action, however, the wealth tax, which has been deemed unconstitutional, will end this year. The states have been hoping to put some form of wealth tax, or offsetting compensation, back into the bill.

Ordinary taxpayers and parents will have reason to cheer if the 1997 bill is not passed. The bill would lower the basic tax deduction and minimum taxable income, and would delay a planned increase in aid to families with children.
The unpopularity solidarity surcharge will also be cut even if the bill is not approved.
